title: Default compose.yml ships gateway with DEV_NO_AUTH=true AND dev-endpoints feature — total JWT bypass
defect: The primary compose.yml builds the gateway image with `CARGO_FEATURES: dev-endpoints` (line 9) and sets `DEV_NO_AUTH: "true"` (line 29), which the publish/subscribe handlers honor to skip JWT verification entirely.
evidence: compose.yml:9 `CARGO_FEATURES: dev-endpoints`; compose.yml:29 `DEV_NO_AUTH: "true"`. routes/publish.rs:55-74 and routes/subscribe.rs:54-63 call `crate::config::dev_no_auth()` and, when true, build a PublishRequest/SubscribeRequest with `bearer_token: String::new()` — no verify() call. This is the default compose file, not compose.ci.yml.
failure_scenario: Anyone deploying via the repo's default `docker compose up` (the obvious path to production) gets a gateway where POST /v1/publish and /ws/v1/subscribe accept unauthenticated requests with an empty token. An attacker publishes forged events into any tenant's channel and subscribes to any channel with no credentials — complete auth and tenant-isolation collapse.
verify_reason:
The mechanism is real and correctly traced. compose.yml:9 sets `CARGO_FEATURES: dev-endpoints`, which the Dockerfile (ARG CARGO_FEATURES) passes to `cargo build --release -p frf-gateway --features dev-endpoints`, compiling the bypass code into the image. compose.yml:29 sets `DEV_NO_AUTH: "true"`. config.rs:66-70 (`dev_no_auth()`, gated by `#[cfg(feature = "dev-endpoints")]`) reads that env var. publish.rs:55-74 and subscribe.rs:54-63 then honor it: they build PublishRequest/SubscribeRequest with `bearer_token: String::new()` and skip both `state.identity.verify()` (JWT) and the Cedar `is_permitted` check entirely. So a gateway built and run from compose.yml accepts unauthenticated publish and subscribe — full auth and tenant-isolation collapse, exactly as described.

The finding is CONFIRMED at CRITICAL severity but its framing is slightly imprecise on one point. The auditor calls compose.yml "the obvious path to production" and implies plain `docker compose up` uses it. In fact a `compose.override.yml` exists and docker compose auto-merges it on `docker compose up`; that override is explicitly a "Minimal dev stack ... auth disabled" that disables keto/flint-gate/postgres/surrealdb via profiles and itself sets DEV_NO_AUTH=true. So the literal default `docker compose up` is a self-declared DEV stack, and the Dockerfile's default build (no CARGO_FEATURES) produces a secure image. The real, still-CRITICAL defect is that compose.yml is production-shaped — it wires real Keto (keto:4466), the flint-gate JWKS URL, JWT_AUDIENCE, and live CDC logical replication, with no dev-only markers in its own body, and the override header even calls it "prod compose.yml" — yet it simultaneously compiles in and activates a total auth bypass. Anyone lifting compose.yml as a production deployment template (via `-f compose.yml` or by deleting the override) ships a gateway where POST /v1/publish and /ws/v1/subscribe accept empty tokens: an attacker forges events into any tenant channel and subscribes to any channel with no credentials. A production-shaped artifact that hard-codes a JWT/Cedar bypass is a legitimate CRITICAL security-config hole; the only correction is that the trigger is "using compose.yml directly" rather than "running the repo's auto-merged default up".

title: Keto check cache key omits tenant_id and namespace → cross-tenant authorization cache poisoning
defect: CacheKey is `(subject, relation, object)` with no tenant_id or namespace component, and the outbound Keto request body (provider.rs:32-39) also never includes tenant_id, so authz decisions are keyed and evaluated flat across tenants.
evidence: cache.rs:7 `pub struct CacheKey(pub String, pub String, pub String);`; provider.rs:52-56 builds the key from `tuple.subject/relation/object` only; provider.rs:32-39 `tuple_body` sends namespace/object/relation/subject_id but drops `tuple.tenant_id`. RelationTuple carries tenant_id (subscribe.rs:52, publish.rs:50) but it is discarded before the wire and before the cache.
failure_scenario: Subject `alice` in tenant A is granted `view` on object `entity-1`; the allow result is cached under `(alice, view, entity-1)`. If tenant B has a subject that resolves to the same subject string and an entity id collision (or channels reuse object ids across tenants), the cached `allow` (TTL 60s) is served for tenant B without ever contacting Keto — cross-tenant read authorization leak that Keto never sees.
verify_reason:
The CODE FACT is real and correctly located. cache.rs:7 defines `CacheKey(subject, relation, object)` with no tenant/namespace component; provider.rs:52-56 builds the cache key from only `tuple.subject/relation/object`; and provider.rs:32-39 `tuple_body` sends `namespace/object/relation/subject_id` and drops `tuple.tenant_id`. RelationTuple does carry tenant_id (authz.rs:9, populated from verified JWT claims at subscribe.rs:52 and publish.rs:50), and it is discarded before both the wire and the cache. The Keto `namespace` is a single static value ("default", set once at gateway startup in main.rs:102-104 / config.rs:84) — not tenant-scoped. All of that is accurate.

HOWEVER, the CRITICAL "cross-tenant cache poisoning / read-authorization leak" failure scenario is not achievable in this codebase, so the severity is overstated. The scenario the prior auditor describes explicitly requires "an entity id collision (or channels reuse object ids across tenants)." But every `object` value fed to authz is a v4 UUID `.to_string()`: subscribe.rs:55 (`channel_id`), subscribe.rs:92 (`envelope.id`), publish.rs:53 (`channel.id`). ChannelId/EntityId/EventId are all `uuid_newtype!` wrappers over `Uuid::new_v4()` (ids.rs:4-57) with no tenant-namespacing and no attacker-controlled or reused form. Two distinct tenants therefore can never legitimately or accidentally share the same `object` string — collision probability is ~2^-122. Because the cache key includes the globally-unique object UUID, a cached `allow` for `(alice, view, entity-1)` can only ever be served for the one real object entity-1, which belongs to exactly one tenant. There is no path to serving tenant A's cached decision for tenant B.

What genuinely remains is a defense-in-depth / correctness gap, not an exploitable leak: (1) tenant_id is silently dropped, so tenant context never reaches Keto and can never be used to scope tuples; (2) the namespace is per-deployment, not per-tenant, so the design leans entirely on object-UUID global uniqueness for isolation, contrary to CLAUDE.md's stated "tenant isolation enforced at the Keto layer." If object ids were ever changed to tenant-relative or human-readable strings (e.g., channel slugs), or if Keto tuples were provisioned into per-tenant namespaces, this flat keying WOULD become a cross-tenant vulnerability — so it is a real latent risk worth fixing (add tenant_id to both CacheKey and the wire body / namespace). But as the code stands today, with v4-UUID objects, the CRITICAL cross-tenant leak does not occur. Correct severity: MEDIUM (latent isolation gap / defense-in-depth), not CRITICAL.

title: No assertion that JWT tenant_id matches the channel/envelope tenant_id on publish or subscribe
defect: PublishUseCase and SubscribePipeline extract the caller's tenant_id from the verified JWT but never compare it to the tenant_id embedded in the target channel/envelope; the only gate is a Keto tuple whose body (see other finding) is itself tenant-flat.
evidence: publish.rs:49-53 builds the publish tuple with `claims.tenant_id` but `object: req.envelope.channel.id.to_string()` — the envelope's own `channel.tenant_id` is never validated against `claims.tenant_id`. Same pattern in subscribe.rs:51-56. grep for `channel.tenant`/`tenant_id ==` across app+routes returns nothing.
failure_scenario: A user with a valid tenant-A JWT crafts a publish whose EventEnvelope.channel.tenant_id = tenant B and channel.id = a tenant-B channel. Because authorization depends solely on a Keto `publish` tuple on the channel object (namespace-flat, and cacheable), if any tuple grants it, the event is written into tenant B's spine under a tenant-B channel — cross-tenant write with no defense-in-depth tenant equality check.
verify_reason: Verified against the actual code. publish.rs:49-54 builds the Keto publish tuple with `tenant_id: claims.tenant_id` but `object: req.envelope.channel.id.to_string()`, then calls `self.broker.publish(req.envelope)` with the full client-supplied envelope — the envelope's own `channel.tenant_id` (frf-domain/src/envelope.rs:10, a public client-controlled field) is never compared to `claims.tenant_id`. subscribe.rs:51-56 has the identical pattern with no tenant-equality assertion. `channel.tenant_id` is fully attacker-controlled on both transports: the gRPC path parses it straight from the client proto (grpc_service.rs:82-86, parse_tenant_id(&ch.tenant_id)) and the HTTP path deserializes the entire EventEnvelope (including channel.tenant_id) directly from the JSON body (routes/publish.rs). Grep for `tenant_id ==` / `channel.tenant` / `assert.*tenant` across frf-app and frf-gateway/src returns no equality check anywhere in the request path. A valid tenant-A caller can therefore submit an envelope with channel.tenant_id = B; if any Keto tuple (and, on HTTP, Cedar policy) grants publish on the target channel object, the event is written into the spine stamped as tenant B and re-emitted with that tenant_id (grpc_service.rs:137) to consumers — a cross-tenant integrity/defense-in-depth hole. This directly violates CLAUDE.md's requirement that tenant isolation be enforced structurally rather than relying solely on a namespace-flat Keto tuple. One minor over-statement in the prior write-up: the HTTP publish path is NOT gated 'solely' by a Keto tuple — it also runs a Cedar is_permitted('Publish', channel_id) check (routes/publish.rs) — but Cedar too is keyed only on claims.tenant_id + channel.id and never on envelope.channel.tenant_id, so the missing equality check stands on both transports and both operations. HIGH severity is correct: exploitation still requires an authz grant on the target channel object, so it is not unconditionally CRITICAL, but the missing app-layer tenant equality assertion is exactly the defense-in-depth the security constraints mandate.

title: SignalService gRPC checks Bearer-token presence only — never verifies the JWT
defect: The signal() RPC extracts the Bearer token into `_token` and discards it without calling identity.verify(); any non-empty `Authorization: Bearer <anything>` value passes, and tenant_id/session are then trusted from the client-supplied envelope.
evidence: signal_service.rs:192-198 binds `let _token = ... .ok_or_else(|| Status::unauthenticated(...))?` then never uses it. proto_to_domain (137) reads tenant_id straight from `proto.tenant_id`. No verify() call exists in this file. (Mitigated: SignalServiceServer is not added in main.rs — only AgentServiceServer is wired at main.rs:347-352 — so it is currently dead code.)
failure_scenario: If any future wiring adds `.add_service(SpineSignalService::...into_server())` to the tonic server (the into_server() helper already exists), the WebRTC signaling plane accepts a literal `Bearer x` and relays offers/answers/ICE for an attacker-chosen tenant_id and session — full media-plane impersonation and cross-tenant signaling with no real authentication.
verify_reason: The code characterization is entirely correct and verified. In crates/frf-gateway/src/signal_service.rs the signal() RPC (lines 191-198) extracts the Bearer token into `_token` via `.ok_or_else(|| Status::unauthenticated("missing Bearer token"))?` and then discards it — there is no verify() call anywhere in the file (grep for verify/IdentityVerifier/identity returns only a comment at line 202). The struct SpineSignalService<M> holds only `signaler: Arc<M>` and has no IdentityVerifier dependency, so it structurally cannot authenticate. proto_to_domain (line 137) trusts tenant_id straight from the client envelope (`TenantId::from_uuid(parse_uuid(&proto.tenant_id, ...))`), and from_session (line 138) likewise. This is a genuine divergence from the correctly-implemented sibling: the wired agent_grpc_service.rs extracts the bearer AND calls `.verify(&bearer_token)` (line 68) against an IdentityVerifier, rejecting on failure — so the pattern to follow already exists and signal_service.rs simply fails to follow it.\n\nSeverity is OVERSTATED as HIGH. The finding's own evidence contains the disqualifier: SignalServiceServer is never instantiated or added to the tonic server. main.rs wires only AgentGrpcService (`.add_service(agent_svc)` at line 352; agent_svc built at line 347), and a grep across the entire gateway shows SpineSignalService referenced only in its own definition and the `pub mod signal_service;` declaration in lib.rs. No request can ever reach signal(), so nothing breaks in production as shipped — there is no reachable media-plane impersonation today. The failure scenario is explicitly conditional ('If any future wiring adds .add_service(...)'), which is a hypothetical future regression, not a current production vulnerability. This is a real latent security landmine (dead code that authenticates incorrectly and would be exploitable the moment it is wired) and worth fixing before it ships live, but as unreachable dead code it does not meet HIGH ('Bug or significant quality issue' affecting production). LOW/NOTE is the accurate rating for an inert, non-wired code path; MEDIUM at most if you weight the ease of accidental future activation.

title: SyncService gRPC has no authentication and trusts client-supplied per-op tenant_id
defect: The sync() bidi RPC and get_checkpoint() perform no Bearer extraction, no identity.verify(), and no authz check; tenant_id and entity_id are parsed directly from each client op and used to read/write CRDT state.
evidence: sync_grpc_service.rs:71-152 sync() never touches request.metadata()/authorization; op.tenant_id (line 98) and op.entity_id (line 91) come straight from the wire and feed `apply_server_delta`. get_checkpoint (156-180) likewise reads req.tenant_id (162) with no auth. (Mitigated: SyncServiceServer is not wired into main.rs.)
failure_scenario: If SyncServiceServer is ever added to the server, any client on the gRPC port can read (get_checkpoint) and mutate (sync apply_server_delta) any tenant's CRDT entity by simply supplying that tenant_id/entity_id — unauthenticated cross-tenant CRDT read/write.
verify_reason: The technical claims are all correct and verified against the code. sync_grpc_service.rs sync() (lines 71-152) and get_checkpoint() (156-180) never touch request.metadata()/authorization, never call identity.verify(), and never perform any authz check; op.entity_id (line 91) and op.tenant_id (line 98) are parsed straight from each client frame and passed into use_case.apply_server_delta (line 117), and get_checkpoint reads req.tenant_id/entity_id (161-162) into use_case.snapshot. The app-layer methods (frf-app/src/sync.rs:79 apply_server_delta, :164 snapshot) do CRDT restore/merge/checkpoint keyed solely on the caller-supplied tenant_id/entity_id with zero authz — so if this service were reachable, any client could read/write any tenant's CRDT entity. This is also a genuine deviation from the codebase pattern: every sibling gRPC service that IS wired (grpc_service.rs:229-234, signal_service.rs:191-197, agent_grpc_service.rs:68/160-165) performs per-handler Bearer extraction and verify() inside the handler, and there is no global tonic interceptor. HOWEVER, the mitigation the auditor already noted is decisive for a release-readiness rating: SyncGrpcService/SyncServiceServer is constructed nowhere. It is only declared as a pub module in lib.rs and referenced within its own file. main.rs:346-358 builds the tonic Server with ONLY .add_service(agent_svc) — SyncServiceServer is never added, and no interceptor path exists. Therefore nothing exploitable ships in the production build; the hole is unreachable until someone later adds `.add_service(sync_svc.into_server())`. For a production-release audit, HIGH overstates a vulnerability that cannot be triggered in the shipped binary. The correct characterization is MEDIUM: dormant/dead code that is a latent security trap — it becomes an unauthenticated cross-tenant CRDT read/write hole the moment it is wired, and it deviates from the auth pattern every other service follows, so it should be gated behind auth (interceptor or in-handler verify) or removed before it is ever enabled.

title: Hardcoded flint-gate JWT signing secret committed in compose.yml
defect: The flint-gate JWT secret is a hardcoded literal in the primary compose file, so every image built from this repo mints and verifies tokens with a publicly-known secret.
evidence: compose.yml:85 `FLINT_GATE_JWT_SECRET: "dev-secret-for-stage-10-integration-testing-only"`. flint-gate is the IdP whose JWKS (GATEWAY_JWKS_URL, compose.yml:19) the gateway trusts to mint/verify all bearer tokens.
failure_scenario: An attacker reads this value from the repo and forges JWTs with arbitrary sub/tenant_id/roles that flint-gate/the gateway accept as valid. Combined with the missing tenant-equality check, they can impersonate any user in any tenant. Even labeled 'testing-only', it is wired into the default compose that doubles as the release path.
verify_reason: The literal fact is CONFIRMED: compose.yml:85 hardcodes `FLINT_GATE_JWT_SECRET: "dev-secret-for-stage-10-integration-testing-only"`. But the HIGH severity and the failure scenario are overstated/mischaracterized. (1) This is provably a local Stage-10 integration-test harness, not a release path: deploy/flint-gate/config.yaml:2 explicitly says "NOT for production. The JWT signing secret is intentionally weak and well-known," and compose.yml:78 builds flint-gate from a hardcoded developer-local absolute path (/Users/gqadonis/Projects/prometheus/flint-gate) that cannot build in CI or on any other machine. No prod/helm/k8s manifests exist in the repo. (2) The gateway does NOT verify tokens with this secret: OryIdentityVerifier fetches an asymmetric JWKS from GATEWAY_JWKS_URL (crates/frf-identity-ory/src/jwks.rs, verifier.rs), whereas the leaked secret is an HS256 symmetric key (deploy/flint-gate/config.yaml:20-21). The auditor's core scenario — forge JWTs the gateway accepts using this secret — is mechanically impossible on the gateway path. (3) In this exact stack the gateway does no auth at all: compose.yml:29 sets DEV_NO_AUTH=true with CARGO_FEATURES=dev-endpoints, and config.rs:65-70 dev_no_auth() fully bypasses JWT verification, so the secret's strength is irrelevant here. (4) flint-gate itself uses dev_passthrough/anonymous auth (config.yaml:37-39, default_subject "dev-integration"), so forging tokens grants nothing beyond the anonymous passthrough. The genuine residual concern is a real-but-LOW hygiene issue (a weak secret and frf:frf DB creds committed, which could be copied into a real deployment); it is not a HIGH production vulnerability. The "combined with missing tenant-equality check, impersonate any user in any tenant" is speculative chaining invalidated by DEV_NO_AUTH and the JWKS/HS256 mismatch.

title: No rate limiting and no CORS policy on any gateway route
defect: build_router constructs the Axum router with zero tower middleware — no CorsLayer, no rate-limit/governor layer, no request-body limit tuning — on publish, subscribe, and agents endpoints.
evidence: lib.rs:63-91 chains only `.route(...)` calls and `.with_state(state)`. grep for `CorsLayer|RateLimit|GovernorLayer|ServiceBuilder|.layer(` across crates/frf-gateway/src returned NONE.
failure_scenario: Each /ws/v1/subscribe upgrade spawns an unbounded Keto-check-per-event stream with no per-client rate cap; an attacker opens thousands of subscribe/publish requests to exhaust gateway and Keto capacity (each event triggers an outbound Keto HTTP call on cache miss). With no CORS policy, browser-origin requests are also ungoverned. No throttling exists to blunt credential-stuffing against the publish/subscribe auth path.
verify_reason: Verified against actual code. build_router (crates/frf-gateway/src/lib.rs:53-92) constructs the Axum router from only `.route(...)` calls plus `.with_state(state)` — no `.layer(...)`, no ServiceBuilder, no CorsLayer, no governor/rate-limit layer, no DefaultBodyLimit/RequestBodyLimit anywhere. grep across all of crates/frf-gateway/src/ confirms zero `.layer(` occurrences, and grep across crates/ confirms zero CorsLayer/GovernorLayer/RateLimit usage. Notably, tower-http IS declared (workspace Cargo.toml:40 with features cors/trace/compression-br; gateway Cargo.toml:54) but is completely unused — middleware was intended and never wired. main.rs:158 serves the bare router via `axum::serve(listener, app)` with no wrapper. The per-event Keto amplification is real: routes/subscribe.rs upgrades then streams via handle_socket, and frf-app/src/subscribe.rs:81-102 runs `authz.check(&view_tuple)` for EVERY envelope where the tuple object is `envelope.id` (unique per event), so the Keto TTL cache (frf-authz-keto/src/cache.rs) never hits for distinct events — one outbound Keto HTTP call per delivered event, with no per-client rate cap. All five technical claims in the finding are accurate. Severity should be raised from MEDIUM to HIGH: on a production-release candidate this is a concrete resource-exhaustion/DoS vector (unbounded subscribe/publish concurrency + per-event backend HTTP amplification) plus a missing CORS policy on a browser-facing gateway and no request-body limit — real operational/security holes, not a style nit. It is not CRITICAL because the worst amplification requires passing the pre-upgrade subscribe auth check and there is no data-loss or RCE component.

title: JWT validation does not verify issuer (iss)
defect: Validation is configured with RS256 and audience only; the issuer claim is never validated and FrfClaims does not even carry `iss`, so any key present in the trusted JWKS can mint accepted tokens regardless of issuer.
evidence: verifier.rs:48-49 `let mut validation = Validation::new(Algorithm::RS256); validation.set_audience(&[&self.audience]);` — no `validation.set_issuer(...)`. claims.rs:10-22 FrfClaims has no `iss` field. exp is validated by jsonwebtoken default, aud is set, but iss/nbf-issuer binding is absent.
failure_scenario: If GATEWAY_JWKS_URL ever serves keys for more than one issuer (multi-tenant IdP, key reuse, or a compromised/rotated-in key from a different Ory project), tokens minted by an unintended issuer with the correct audience are accepted. There is no issuer allowlist to contain blast radius of a mis-scoped JWKS.
verify_reason: Verified against source: crates/frf-identity-ory/src/verifier.rs:48-49 constructs `Validation::new(Algorithm::RS256)` and calls only `validation.set_audience(&[&self.audience])` — there is no `validation.set_issuer(...)`. crates/frf-identity-ory/src/claims.rs:10-22 defines FrfClaims with sub/email/tenant_id/roles/jti/aud/exp and NO `iss` field, so issuer is never deserialized or checked. I confirmed the absence is systemic, not compensated elsewhere: a repo-wide grep found no `set_issuer` or issuer handling anywhere, and the gateway carries no issuer config — frf-gateway/src/config.rs only reads GATEWAY_JWKS_URL and JWT_AUDIENCE, and frf-gateway/src/main.rs:106-109 constructs OryIdentityVerifier::new(jwks_url, audience) with no issuer argument. exp is validated by jsonwebtoken defaults and aud is enforced, but iss is not. The defect and evidence are accurately characterized. Severity MEDIUM is correct, not overstated: this is a defense-in-depth / hardening gap (RFC 8725 recommends validating iss), NOT an active auth bypass in the documented topology, because per CLAUDE.md flint-gate is the sole JWT minting authority and GATEWAY_JWKS_URL points at a single-issuer endpoint. It only becomes exploitable under the auditor's stated preconditions — a multi-issuer/shared JWKS, key reuse, or a compromised/rotated-in key from another Ory project — at which point any key in the trusted JWKS with the correct audience yields an accepted token with no issuer allowlist to contain blast radius. Real and correctly scoped as MEDIUM.

title: Federation bridges ingest events under a fresh random tenant_id each boot
defect: Matrix and ATProto bridges are constructed with `TenantId::new()` / `ChannelId::new()`, which generate random v4 UUIDs, so all federated events are stamped with a random, non-deterministic tenant/channel that changes on every restart.
evidence: main.rs:192 `MatrixBridge::new(client, room, TenantId::new(), ChannelId::new())`; main.rs:199 `AtProtoBridge::new(url, collections, TenantId::new(), ChannelId::new())`. These bridged events are published to the spine via spawn_federation_ingest_tasks (main.rs:229) with that random tenant stamped by convert.rs.
failure_scenario: Federated Matrix/ATProto messages land under a random tenant id that no real subscriber's JWT tenant_id will match, so either the data is orphaned (silent data loss / federation appears broken) or, worse, collides with a legitimate tenant UUID and injects untrusted external content into that tenant's channel. Either way the federation ingest tenant assignment is a hardcoded placeholder, not a real tenant binding.
verify_reason: Verified real and correctly located. crates/frf-domain/src/ids.rs:13-14 defines TenantId::new()/ChannelId::new() as Uuid::new_v4() (random). crates/frf-gateway/src/main.rs:192 (MatrixBridge::new) and :199 (AtProtoBridge::new) construct both federation bridges with TenantId::new()/ChannelId::new() — random UUIDs regenerated every boot. There is NO config field to supply a real tenant: config.rs exposes matrix_homeserver_url/matrix_room_id/atproto_jetstream_url etc. but no matrix_tenant_id or atproto_tenant_id. Both convert.rs files (frf-bridge-matrix/src/convert.rs:24-28, frf-bridge-atproto/src/convert.rs) stamp Channel { id: channel_id, tenant_id, path } from those constructor IDs onto every ingested envelope, which spawn_federation_ingest_tasks (main.rs:229) publishes to the broker. IggyBroker::publish (frf-broker-iggy/src/broker.rs:49-50) routes to stream_name(envelope.channel.tenant_id) = "tenant-{random-uuid}", so federated events land on a stream keyed by a random UUID that changes every restart and that no real subscriber reads — silent federation data loss / broken federation. The smoking-gun contrast: the CDC consumer path (main.rs:264-276) REQUIRES CDC_TENANT_ID config and hard-fails startup if absent (TenantId::from_uuid(config.cdc_tenant_id)), proving federation's random IDs are an unwired placeholder, not a deliberate design. One nuance makes the auditor's framing slightly overstated: the "collides with a legitimate tenant and injects untrusted content into that tenant's channel" half is largely theoretical — v4 UUID collision with a real tenant is astronomically improbable, and even then the per-event Keto 'view' authz check (subscribe.rs:88-94, keyed on envelope.id) gates delivery, and the broker fans out subscribers by channel-{channel_id} (broker.rs:82-86) not tenant. The dominant, correct real-world outcome is orphaning/silent data loss, not a live cross-tenant breach. MEDIUM severity is correctly calibrated for a broken-federation / silent-data-loss defect that is not an exploitable security hole.

title: str0m 'sovereign SFU' is a fake — str0m crate never imported, no Rtc/SDP/ICE; bare in-memory message router
defect: StrOmSignaler implements MediaSignaler as an in-memory DashMap<(tenant,session), mpsc::Sender> relay with zero WebRTC logic; the str0m crate declared in Cargo.toml is never imported (no `use str0m`, no Rtc, no SDP/ICE handling), and the doc comment references process_offer/process_ice methods that do not exist in the file.
evidence: grep 'use str0m|Rtc|process_offer|process_ice' over frf-media-str0m/src returns only doc-comment matches at sfu.rs:32; Cargo.toml line str0m={workspace=true} is a phantom dependency; send_signal at sfu.rs:56-68 only forwards the envelope to a session mpsc channel.
failure_scenario: Gateway boots with SfuMode::Sovereign (main.rs:311 wires StrOmSignaler::new()). A WebRTC client sends an SDP offer; the adapter routes the JSON envelope to another session's channel but never negotiates a peer connection, never produces an SDP answer, never forwards RTP. No media ever flows. The 'sovereign SFU' plane is non-functional in production while appearing wired and healthy.
verify_reason: Verified against actual code. crates/frf-media-str0m/src/sfu.rs (the only substantive file, 175 lines) contains zero WebRTC logic: StrOmSignaler is Arc<DashMap<(TenantId,SessionId), SfuSession>> where SfuSession is just an mpsc::Sender + Instant. send_signal (sfu.rs:56-68) forwards the envelope to a session channel; subscribe_signals returns a ReceiverStream; remove_session drops the entry. Grep for str0m/Rtc/SDP/ICE/RTP/Media across crates/frf-media-str0m/src/ returns ONLY doc-comment and #[instrument] name matches — there is no `use str0m::...` anywhere. The str0m dependency in both the crate Cargo.toml (str0m={workspace=true}) and workspace root (str0m="0.7", Cargo.toml:109) is a provably-dead phantom dependency. The doc comment (sfu.rs:31-33) claims the Rtc state machine is driven externally via process_offer/process_ice, but neither method exists in the crate or the MediaSignaler port. main.rs:311 unconditionally wires StrOmSignaler::new() under SfuMode::Sovereign (confirmed verbatim), logging "SFU mode: sovereign (str0m)". title: Matrix inbound federation stream is hardcoded stream::empty() — zero events ever delivered, yet wired into gateway

However CRITICAL is overstated. (1) Only INBOUND is dead — MatrixBridge::send performs a real PUT to /_matrix/client/v3/rooms/{room}/send/m.room.message/{txn}, so outbound projection works. title: ATProto outbound send() is a hard Err — outbound Bluesky federation structurally impossible

title: Cedar action policy: Entities::empty() + blanket permit-all default policy = authorize-everything
defect: is_permitted always evaluates against Entities::empty(), so no principal/resource attributes or group hierarchy exist — any Cedar policy using `principal.x`, `resource.y`, or `in` conditions silently evaluates to Deny. Compounding this, the bundled default policy.cedar is an unconditional permit for Publish and Subscribe with no principal/resource constraints.
evidence: lib.rs:91 `self.authorizer.is_authorized(&request, &self.policy_set, &Entities::empty())`; policy.cedar contains only `permit(principal, action == Action::"Publish", resource);` and the same for Subscribe with no conditions.
failure_scenario: Two failure modes. (a) With the shipped default policy, CedarPolicyEngine::new() authorizes every Publish/Subscribe from every principal on every resource — the mutation-policy (PAUX-1) layer is a no-op allow-all. (b) If an operator writes a real attribute-based policy (e.g. permit when resource.owner == principal), it can never match because no entities are supplied, so all mutating actions are silently denied — a correctness cliff with no error surfaced.
verify_reason:
Both mechanics are verified in the actual code. (a) crates/frf-policy-cedar/src/policy.cedar contains only two unconditional permits — `permit(principal, action == Action::"Publish", resource);` and the same for Subscribe — with zero principal/resource/context constraints; CedarPolicyEngine::new() (lib.rs:37-39) loads this via include_str!, so is_permitted returns Allow for every Publish/Subscribe from every tenant on every resource. The publish route (routes/publish.rs:89-107) does call and honor is_permitted, but the check always passes, making the PAUX-1 mutation-policy layer a no-op allow-all when Cedar is enabled. (b) lib.rs:91 always passes &Entities::empty() to is_authorized, and the is_permitted signature only accepts &str action/resource + TenantId — there is no path to inject entity attributes or group hierarchy, so any operator-authored attribute-based policy (principal.x / resource.y / `in`) can never match and silently evaluates to Deny with no error surfaced. Both failure modes are real and correctly characterized.

Two facts temper the 'authorize-everything' severity but do not refute the finding: (1) POLICY_ENGINE defaults to None → NoOpPolicyProvider in both from_env (config.rs:191-198) and test_default (config.rs:101), so Cedar is opt-in; the allow-all only appears when an operator deliberately sets POLICY_ENGINE=cedar expecting enforcement. (2) This is the Cedar action/mutation-policy (PAUX-1) layer only; per CLAUDE.md tenant isolation and per-event visibility are enforced separately at the Keto layer (wired unconditionally), so this does not defeat tenant isolation — it defeats mutating-action authorization. The policy.cedar file is also explicitly documented as a placeholder to replace in production. HIGH is the correct severity: the Entities::empty() design makes the layer structurally incapable of the attribute/relationship-based authorization Cedar exists to provide, so an operator enabling Cedar gets either silent allow-all (default policy) or silent deny-all (any real attribute policy) — a security-relevant correctness cliff. Not CRITICAL because it is opt-in, does not bypass Keto isolation, and ships with a documented placeholder policy.

title: WASM CRDT merge silently returns empty snapshot on peer-delta failure, corrupting client state

The doc-comment even admits 'Returns an empty Vec<u8> on merge error (callers should check length > 0)', pushing an easily-forgotten invariant onto JS callers.

If the JS caller does not check length>0, it overwrites the local snapshot with empty bytes, silently wiping the entity's CRDT state on that device; on next export the device pushes an empty/rolled-back document to peers, propagating data loss.
verify_reason:
The code is real and correctly quoted. crates/frf-wasm/src/crdt.rs:17 is `frf_crdt::apply_delta(snapshot, delta).unwrap_or_default()`, and apply_delta (crates/frf-crdt/src/merge.rs:17-30) returns Result<Vec<u8>, CrdtError>, mapping Loro decode/merge/encode failures to typed errors. So a malformed/version-incompatible peer delta is genuinely swallowed into an empty Vec<u8>, and the doc-comment (crdt.rs:9-10) admits this and pushes a length>0 check onto callers. The sibling FFI binding (crates/frf-ffi/src/crdt.rs:15-16) correctly propagates the Result, confirming the WASM binding is an inconsistent outlier that erases the error contract. The DEFECT is CONFIRMED as a real, legitimate finding (silent error swallowing / fragile caller-side invariant).

However, the MEDIUM severity and the failure narrative ("silently wiping the entity's CRDT state on that device... propagating data loss to peers") are OVERSTATED relative to actual reachability. The only real JS/TS consumer is admin-ui/src/features/signaling/components/CrdtDemoButton.tsx, which calls crdt_apply_delta([], []) with empty inputs and merely renders the returned byte count — it never feeds a peer-controlled delta and never persists the result to local CRDT state. The admin-ui dev build resolves "frf-wasm" to a stub that throws (admin-ui/vite.config.ts:30-37); the real WASM is only produced by a manual build script. No production code path today overwrites a device snapshot with this output, so the "corrupts client state / propagates data loss" chain is not currently reachable — it is a latent trap for a future caller, not a live corruption bug. Correct severity is LOW: a real correctness/API-contract defect (unwrap_or_default hides errors, inconsistent with the FFI sibling, invariant offloaded to callers) that should be fixed before the WASM CRDT path is wired into real state, but not an active data-loss vulnerability.

title: redb mark_synced swallows per-entry read errors via entry.ok()?, potentially leaking un-acked ops
defect: Inside the delete-collection filter, `let (k, _) = entry.ok()?;` discards a redb range-read error for that entry, so a transient storage error causes the key to be skipped from the synced-deletion set instead of failing the transaction.
evidence: store.rs:156-157 `read.filter_map(|entry| { let (k, _) = entry.ok()?; ... })` — compare with drain_pending (line 119) which correctly uses `entry.map_err(RedbOpStoreError::Storage)?`. The two iterators over the same table handle entry errors inconsistently.
failure_scenario: During mark_synced, a redb read error on one entry (e.g. transient I/O) makes ok()? yield None; that op is silently excluded from keys_to_delete and stays in the pending op-log after being server-confirmed. The op is then re-drained and re-sent on the next sync cycle, causing duplicate op delivery to the server; because the transaction still commits Ok, the caller never learns the ack was partial.
verify_reason: The code defect is real and accurately located. At crates/frf-store-redb/src/store.rs:157, inside mark_synced's delete-collection filter_map, `let (k, _) = entry.ok()?;` discards the redb range-read Result<_, StorageError> and returns None from the closure. filter_map treats that None identically to a non-matching entry, so an entry whose read errored is silently excluded from keys_to_delete and remains in the pending_ops table, while wtx.commit() still returns Ok(()) and the caller (frf-app/src/sync.rs:112) sees success. This is genuinely inconsistent with the sibling code: drain_pending (line 119) uses `entry.map_err(RedbOpStoreError::Storage)?` and the remove loop in the same function (lines 173-175) also propagates, so the same table's range iterator is handled two different ways. The error type is redb::StorageError (confirmed in error.rs), the same class both other sites propagate — so the auditor's core claim (inconsistent per-entry error handling that can leak an already-acked op back into the pending log) is correct.\n\nHowever the failure scenario is somewhat overstated in impact, which is why LOW (the auditor's own severity) is right and should not be raised. (1) The trigger is narrow: a StorageError mid-range-read implies I/O failure or on-disk corruption, in which case the subsequent remove()/commit() would very likely also fail and abort the whole transaction; the silent-partial-commit path needs a transient read error on exactly one entry that does not also break the write/commit. (2) The consequence is not state corruption: sync.rs step 5 only counts remaining.len() (does not itself re-send); ops carry a monotonic per-device local_seq and the entire op-log/CRDT design is idempotent, so any eventual re-delivery of an already-confirmed op converges to the same state — the realistic worst case is a lingering op, a redundant re-send, and an inflated remaining_ops count, not duplicate/incorrect data. (3) The failure direction is the safe one: the op is retained (at-least-once), not dropped, so no data loss. So it is a legitimate robustness/consistency defect that should propagate the error and abort the transaction, but its production blast radius is milder than the 'duplicate op delivery to the server' framing implies. CONFIRMED, severity LOW.

title: Malformed jti in verified JWT is silently replaced with a random session id instead of rejected
defect: Uuid::parse_str(jti).unwrap_or_else(|_| Uuid::new_v4()) fabricates a fresh random SessionId when the token's jti claim is present but not a valid UUID, decoupling the session id from the token identity.
evidence: claims.rs:37-42: `if let Some(jti) = &claims.jti { let jti_uuid = Uuid::parse_str(jti).unwrap_or_else(|_| Uuid::new_v4()); SessionId::from_uuid(jti_uuid) }`. Every other claim (tenant_id at :30-35) is strictly validated and errors on parse failure; jti is uniquely lenient.
failure_scenario: A token minted by flint-gate with a non-UUID jti (or a malformed/attacker-crafted token that passed signature verification but has a garbage jti) is accepted and assigned a brand-new random session id on each request. Session-scoped state (per-session subscription cursors, revocation, dedup) can no longer be correlated to the token, and per-request session ids defeat any session-based rate-limit or revocation keyed on jti.
verify_reason:
The defect is REAL and precisely located. At crates/frf-identity-ory/src/claims.rs:38 the code is exactly `let jti_uuid = Uuid::parse_str(jti).unwrap_or_else(|_| Uuid::new_v4());` — a present-but-malformed jti is silently replaced with a fresh random UUID per request rather than rejected. This is genuinely inconsistent with the surrounding code: tenant_id one branch up (claims.rs:34-35) does `Uuid::parse_str(&tenant_id_str).map_err(|_| IdentityError::MissingClaim(...))?`, strictly erroring on a bad UUID. So jti is uniquely lenient, as claimed. The session_id derived from jti does flow into real state: it becomes `consumer_id` at frf-app/src/subscribe.rs:71 (`claims.session_id.to_string()`), which keys the broker subscription/cursor — so a per-request random session id does decouple the cursor from token identity and breaks session-cursor correlation. LOW severity is appropriate and NOT inflated, which is why the verdict is CONFIRMED rather than OVERSTATED.

However, two parts of the failure scenario are overstated and should not be relied on: (1) The "attacker-crafted token that passed signature verification but has a garbage jti" vector is neutralized upstream — verifier.rs:48-52 enforces RS256 signature via JWKS, audience, and exp before to_verified_claims runs, so an external attacker cannot craft such a token; the realistic trigger is flint-gate itself minting a non-UUID/absent jti (a self-inflicted contract-drift / config risk, not an external exploit). (2) The revocation and session-based rate-limit consequences are unsubstantiated — grep found no revocation store or rate-limiter keyed on jti/session_id anywhere in frf-gateway or frf-app; only the broker consumer/cursor use is backed by code. Net: a genuine LOW correctness/consistency bug (lenient parse of a security-adjacent claim), correctly severity-rated, but with an overstated attacker-exploitability and speculative revocation/rate-limit blast radius.

title: SurrealDB checkpoint store never creates the UNIQUE index it documents; UPSERT-on-table appends duplicate rows per checkpoint
defect: checkpoint() issues `UPSERT type::table($table) SET ... WHERE entity_id=$eid AND tenant_id=$tid` against a table target with no record id and no actual UNIQUE index ever created (the DEFINE INDEX in the doc-comment at line 26 is never executed anywhere in the codebase), so SurrealDB creates a NEW auto-id record on every checkpoint where the WHERE does not select an existing record by id, rather than updating in place.

The crdt_snapshots table grows without bound (one row per sync, forever). restore()'s `ORDER BY version DESC LIMIT 1` hides the duplication functionally but every restore now scans an ever-growing row set (read amplification), storage bloats indefinitely, and there is zero uniqueness enforcement — if two concurrent checkpoints assign the same new_version, restore's ordering is non-deterministic and can resurrect an older/wrong snapshot, corrupting the entity's converged state.
evidence: store.rs:53-68 UPSERT with field-based WHERE on a table target; store.rs:26 `DEFINE INDEX idx_entity_tenant ... UNIQUE` exists ONLY in a doc-comment; grep across crates/ confirms NO DEFINE INDEX/TABLE/FIELD is ever executed; restore() at store.rs:86-87 defensively uses ORDER BY version DESC LIMIT 1, confirming the author anticipates multiple rows per key.
verify_reason:
The finding's central mechanical claim is FALSE, but it surfaces a real (narrower) defect, so it is OVERSTATED rather than a clean false positive.

VERIFIED FACTS:
- store.rs:53-58 issues `UPSERT type::table($table) SET entity_id=$eid, tenant_id=$tid, ... WHERE entity_id=$eid AND tenant_id=$tid` — a table target (no record id), no unique index.
- The `DEFINE INDEX idx_entity_tenant ... UNIQUE` and all DEFINE statements exist ONLY in the doc-comment (store.rs:19-30). `grep -rn "DEFINE INDEX|DEFINE TABLE|DEFINE FIELD"` across crates/ returns only those doc-comment lines. The crate (error.rs, lib.rs, store.rs, model.rs — 181 lines total) has NO migration/init/schema-execution logic. The doc-comment's claim "auto-created on first write — no migration required" is false: SurrealDB does not create UNIQUE indexes from doc-comments. So the "index never created" sub-claim is CORRECT.

WHY THE CORE CLAIM IS FALSE (decisive evidence = official SurrealDB UPSERT docs, verified against surrealdb 3.1.5 in Cargo.lock):
The auditor claims UPSERT-on-a-table-with-field-WHERE "creates a NEW auto-id record on every checkpoint... one row per sync, forever." SurrealDB's documented semantics for exactly this form (UPSERT <table> SET ... WHERE cond, no id specified): "When using the WHERE clause and no specified ID, SurrealDB will check to see if any records match the clause. If nothing matches, a new record will be created... Since a record with the name 'Jaime' exists, an UPSERT followed by WHERE name='Jaime' will UPDATE the existing record instead of creating a new one." Thus for the auditor's own scenario (an entity synced repeatedly = a STABLE entity_id/tenant_id key): 1st checkpoint creates one row; every subsequent checkpoint MATCHES that row via the WHERE and UPDATES IT IN PLACE. No per-sync duplication, no unbounded growth, no read amplification. The claimed production failure ("crdt_snapshots grows without bound, one row per sync forever") does NOT occur. The downstream cascade (non-deterministic restore resurrecting a wrong/older snapshot, corrupting converged state) is predicated on that false premise; restore()'s `ORDER BY version DESC LIMIT 1` returns the highest-version row regardless.

THE GENUINE RESIDUAL DEFECT (why not a full FALSE_POSITIVE, and why LOW not HIGH):
The UPSERT update-in-place guarantee holds only because the WHERE matches the single pre-existing row. Without the UNIQUE index there is a real but NARROW race: two checkpoints for a brand-new (entity_id, tenant_id) executing concurrently before either commits both see zero matching rows and each INSERTs a row -> duplicate rows for that key. The missing UNIQUE index is exactly what would prevent this. This is a legitimate latent concurrency/data-integrity bug and a real doc-vs-actual gap, but it requires concurrent FIRST-writes for the same key (not "every sync"), it self-heals functionally under restore's ORDER BY, and this adapter is not even wired into frf-gateway's main.rs (only InMemoryCrdtStore is used at present), further limiting production exposure. Severity corrected from HIGH to LOW: the described high-impact failure mode is wrong; the actual defect is a narrow, non-default-path race plus a misleading doc-comment.

title: redb composite-key upper bound increments the wrong segment (tenant, not key tail) → empty range scan on all-0xFF tenant → silent op-log data loss
defect: make_prefix_end() computes the exclusive range upper bound by incrementing bytes 16..32 (the TENANT UUID region) of the 40-byte `entity|tenant|seq` key with carry; when that region is 0xFF..0xFF the carry propagates out and the function returns an all-zero-tenant prefix that is LESS THAN make_prefix() (the range start), so redb's range(start..end) yields an empty iterator.
failure_scenario: A tenant whose UUID has 0xFF in the relevant bytes writes offline ops via queue_op (persisted fine). On reconnect, drain_pending builds range(make_prefix .. make_prefix_end); because end < start the scan returns ZERO ops even though they exist on disk — the entire pending offline op-log for that entity is silently dropped and never sent to the server (permanent local data loss / lost edits). Symmetrically mark_synced's scan is empty so it prunes nothing, and for near-boundary tenant UUIDs the incremented-tenant bound can widen the scan into an adjacent tenant's keyspace, a tenant-isolation concern. Correct implementation must increment the trailing byte of the full 32-byte prefix, not the tenant field.
evidence: key.rs:9 layout entity(16)|tenant(16)|seq(8); key.rs:31-45 loop iterates buf[16..32].rev() (tenant bytes) with carry and no clamp; simulated: tenant=0xFF*16 gives end=00..00 < start=..FF..FF → range empty. store.rs:113-114 and 154-155 both depend on this bound for drain_pending and mark_synced.
verify_reason:
CONFIRMED as a real bug with correct root-cause, but HIGH severity overstates production likelihood; MEDIUM is accurate.

MECHANICS (all verified):
- key.rs:31-45: make_prefix_end() increments buf[16..32] — the TENANT UUID region of the 32-byte prefix — with carry and no clamp, instead of incrementing the trailing byte of the full prefix. This is objectively the wrong field.
- Simulated: tenant=0xFF*16 → end=<entity>|00..00 which is LESS THAN start=<entity>|FF..FF, so redb range(start..end) yields an EMPTY iterator. Confirmed exactly as claimed.
- store.rs:113-114 (drain_pending) and 154-155 (mark_synced) both build range(prefix_start..prefix_end) and depend on this bound. Empty range ⇒ drain_pending returns zero ops (silent local op-log loss / dropped offline edits) and mark_synced prunes nothing. Confirmed.
- Secondary tenant-widening claim (tenant UUID ending in 0xFF, ~1/256 per trailing byte) is real: the exclusive upper bound spills past the tenant boundary. Practical impact is bounded because drain_pending re-tags ops with the CALLER's tenant/entity (store.rs:126) and mark_synced deletes by exact key, but it is still a latent correctness/isolation smell.

WHY OVERSTATED (not HIGH):
- The catastrophic 'silent op-log data loss' path requires a tenant UUID of all-0xFF (or the range-inversion boundary). TenantId is normally Uuid::new_v4() (frf-domain/src/ids.rs:14), so the dominant production path never hits the boundary (P≈2^-128) — which is exactly why the existing prefix_end_greater_than_prefix test passes.
- The boundary IS reachable only if caller-controlled tenant UUIDs are accepted: frf-agentproto/src/convert.rs:24 builds TenantId::from_uuid() from a client-supplied proto string. That keeps it from being a pure false positive, but a maliciously/accidentally all-FF tenant UUID is an edge input, not the common case.

NET: genuine, correctly-diagnosed defect in a persistence primitive with a trivial correct fix (increment the trailing byte of the 32-byte prefix, or use redb length-delimited range end). Worth fixing, but the data-loss trigger is an input boundary the primary random-v4 path never produces, so MEDIUM, not HIGH.

Every other SDK (TS/Go/C#/Swift/Kotlin/Dart) must re-derive or omit this logic — and all of them omit it — so 'business logic in one place' has no place at all and the FFI/wasm SDKs cannot inherit reconnection behavior in production.

verify_reason: Verified REAL and correctly characterized as CRITICAL for a production-release audit. Evidence: (1) `ls crates/frf-sdk-rust` -> "No such file or directory"; the crate is absent, is not a workspace member (no `sdk` entry in Cargo.toml members), and appears only in docs (CLAUDE.md:61/240, README.md:220, docs/IMPLEMENTATION-PLAN.md:72/172/304). title: No SDK in any language implements reconnection/backoff/retry — permanent disconnect on any network blip
defect: A repo-wide search for reconnect/backoff/retry across all SDK sources (ts, go, csharp, dart, swift, kotlin) returns zero matches; subscribe() just yields the raw Connect/gRPC stream with no resubscribe-on-drop logic.
failure_scenario: In production, a mobile client or browser on flaky WiFi has its subscribe stream terminated by a transient network error or gateway restart. The SpineClient.subscribe async-iterable simply ends; the app stops receiving events silently and never reconnects or replays from its last offset, causing permanent data staleness until the app is manually restarted.
evidence: `grep -rniE 'reconnect|backoff|retry' sdks (excluding node_modules/build/dist)` -> no results; sdks/ts/src/client.ts subscribe() returns this.inner.subscribe(req) directly; sdks/go/client/spine_client.go Subscribe returns raw ServerStreamForClient; sdks/csharp SpineClient.SubscribeAsync loops MoveNext with no retry.
verify_reason: Verified by reading actual code. sdks/ts/src/client.ts subscribe() returns this.inner.subscribe(req) with no resubscribe/backoff; sdks/go/client/spine_client.go Subscribe() returns the raw *connect.ServerStreamForClient with no retry; sdks/csharp/FlintSdk/Client/SpineClient.cs:34-43 SubscribeAsync is a bare `while(await MoveNext(ct)) yield` loop that silently ends on stream drop. Repo-wide grep for reconnect|backoff|retry across ts/go/csharp/dart/swift/kotlin sources returns ZERO matches; dart/swift/kotlin are single-file scaffolds with no client logic to hide such code. The failure scenario is real: on any transient network error or gateway restart the stream terminates and the client stops receiving events with no auto-reconnect. This is corroborated and made worse by the frozen contract: proto/flint/v1/envelope.proto explicitly provides resumable subscription (SubscribeRequest.from = Offset) and offset-carrying AckRequest — the exact replay primitives a reconnect would use exist but no SDK consumes them. Severity HIGH is correct: it is a genuine missing-functionality/does-not-connect production defect affecting every SDK consumer, but it is not a security or data-corruption issue, and application authors technically can hand-roll reconnection on the exposed offset primitives, so CRITICAL would be over-stated. The cited line anchor (client.ts:27, the subscribe method) is accurate.

title: All real SDKs (TS/Go/C#) cover only SpineService — 5 of 6 proto services are unbound

(2) sdks/go/client/spine_client.go defines only SpineClient wrapping flintv1connect.SpineServiceClient (Publish/Subscribe). If anything the finding is understated — the gateway's native gRPC server (crates/frf-gateway/src/main.rs:347-353) registers ONLY agent_svc via .add_service(agent_svc); Spine/Sync/Signal/Entity/Authz define into_server() but are never added to the tonic router, and EntityService/AuthzService have no HTTP/WS route either, so those services are unreachable server-side as well. title: SDK clients inject no JWT/auth header despite gateway requiring flint-gate JWT verification
defect: The Go, C#, and TS SpineClient constructors provide no mechanism to attach an Authorization/Bearer JWT; Go uses http.DefaultClient with no interceptor, C# uses GrpcChannel.ForAddress with no credentials, TS takes a bare Transport, so calls go out unauthenticated by default.
failure_scenario: Because the gateway verifies JWTs via flint-gate (GATEWAY_JWKS_URL) on every request, all SDK publish/subscribe calls are rejected with 401 unless the caller manually and undocumentedly wires an interceptor. The go smoke_test even comments 'expected error without auth', confirming the default path is unauthenticated and non-functional against a secured gateway.
evidence: sdks/go/client/spine_client.go line 22 `flintv1connect.NewSpineServiceClient(http.DefaultClient, baseURL, opts...)`; sdks/csharp SpineClient.Create uses GrpcChannel.ForAddress(address) with no ChannelCredentials; `grep bearer|jwt|token sdks/*/src` -> only CancellationToken; sdks/go/client/smoke_test.go: 'publish returned (expected error without auth)'.
verify_reason: The finding is REAL in substance: the gateway enforces JWT on every SDK-facing path (grpc_service.rs:227-234 returns Status::unauthenticated when the `authorization` metadata is missing; routes/publish.rs:76-83 returns 401 without an `Authorization: Bearer` header then verifies the JWT), and no SDK ships a built-in or documented way to attach a token. A grep across sdks/go, sdks/ts/src, and sdks/csharp for bearer|jwt|token|Interceptor|CallCredentials|Metadata yields only a Go comment and CancellationToken. The go smoke_test.go:22 comment "expected error without auth" confirms the default path is unauthenticated and non-functional against the secured gateway. HOWEVER the blanket claim "provide no mechanism to attach a JWT" is inaccurate for 2 of the 3 SDKs: sdks/go/client/spine_client.go:20-22 forwards `opts ...connect.ClientOption` (a caller CAN attach a Connect interceptor that injects the header — the code comment at line 19 even says so), and sdks/ts/src/client.ts:16-22 takes a bare `Transport` the caller constructs, which can carry an auth interceptor. Only the C# client (sdks/csharp/FlintSdk/Client/SpineClient.cs:18-22, `Create(string address)` using GrpcChannel.ForAddress with no credentials and no options passthrough) genuinely exposes NO mechanism. So this is a real DX/missing-helper gap plus a C#-specific functional blocker — not a security hole (the gateway correctly rejects unauthenticated calls, which is the secure behavior). Severity HIGH is overstated for the aggregate claim; the correct framing is a MEDIUM ergonomics/documentation defect (with the C# no-auth-passthrough being the one hard blocker).

title: CRDT logic is duplicated across three independent Rust surfaces instead of one
defect: CRDT byte-blob operations are exposed independently by frf-ffi (Swift/Kotlin/Dart), frf-wasm (browser TS), and frf-crdt (core), while publish/subscribe transport is re-implemented separately in frf-wasm (WebSocket/HTTP) vs. the Connect/gRPC generated clients — contradicting the 'exactly one place' invariant.
failure_scenario: A behavioral fix to CRDT merge or the subscribe channel/token wire format must be applied and re-verified in multiple places (frf-wasm subscribe.rs builds ws URL `?channel=&token=` while gateway/proto SubscribeRequest uses channel_id/consumer_id/from). Drift between the wasm WebSocket path and the Connect path means the same 'subscribe' means different things per SDK, producing inconsistent client behavior in production.
evidence: frf-wasm/src/{crdt,publish,subscribe}.rs implement crdt+http+ws directly; frf-ffi/src/crdt.rs implements crdt again for UniFFI; frf-wasm subscribe.rs builds `/ws/v1/subscribe?channel=...&token=...` whereas proto SubscribeRequest fields are channel_id/consumer_id/from and TS SpineClient uses Connect unary/stream, not that WS path.
verify_reason:
Mixed: the finding's headline ("CRDT logic is duplicated across three independent Rust surfaces") is INACCURATE/overstated, but the embedded transport-drift failure scenario is REAL (and understated). Evidence:

DUPLICATION CLAIM = FALSE. The core Loro merge lives in exactly one place: frf-crdt/src/merge.rs:17 `pub fn apply_delta`. Both other surfaces are thin delegating shims, not re-implementations: frf-wasm/src/crdt.rs:17 calls `frf_crdt::apply_delta(...)` (a ~6-line wrapper whose own docstring says "the merge logic lives in frf-crdt"), and frf-ffi/src/crdt.rs:16 calls `frf_crdt::apply_delta(...)`. This is the correct WASM/UniFFI boundary pattern, not duplicated CRDT logic. The finding's evidence line ("frf-wasm implements crdt directly; frf-ffi implements crdt again") is wrong. The only minor real divergence is frf-ffi/crdt.rs:27,40 (`crdt_new_snapshot`/`crdt_snapshot_version`) calling `loro::` directly instead of via a core helper — cosmetic, not a merge-logic fork.

TRANSPORT DRIFT = REAL and CONFIRMED (this is the load-bearing part of the failure scenario). frf-wasm's publish/subscribe do not connect to the gateway as written and diverge from the TS Connect path:
- SUBSCRIBE: gateway routes/subscribe.rs reads `?channel=` (matches wasm) but (a) parses it as a UUID (line 71 → 400 for wasm's exemplified `entity/my-room`), and (b) takes the token ONLY from the `Authorization: Bearer` header (bearer_token(), lines 23-29, 66) and never reads a `?token=` query param — yet frf-wasm/src/subscribe.rs:26 appends `?token={t}` because a browser WebSocket cannot set headers. Result: token silently dropped → 401.
- PUBLISH: gateway routes/publish.rs:45 takes `Json(envelope): Json<EventEnvelope>` and derives channel from `envelope.channel.id` (line 88); it never reads any channel header (grep for X-Channel-Path in gateway returns zero matches). frf-wasm/src/publish.rs:22,34 posts an arbitrary JSON `payload` (not an EventEnvelope) and puts the channel in an `X-Channel-Path` header → body fails deserialization, channel lost.
- The TS SDK uses a different transport entirely: sdks/ts/src/client.ts:17,28 `createPromiseClient(SpineService, transport)` (Connect), not the WS `?channel=&token=` path.

So the transport-mismatch defect is genuine and arguably HIGH (the wasm browser client is non-functional against the current gateway), but the finding as titled/framed (CRDT duplication across three surfaces) mischaracterizes it. Keeping corrected severity at MEDIUM to match the finding's original severity since the real defect is a wire-format/drift issue between an SDK surface and the gateway, not a security or data-loss issue.

title: C# SDK commits its own copy of proto files, forking the frozen contract source of truth
defect: The C# project compiles from sdks/csharp/FlintSdk/proto/flint/v1/*.proto — a duplicated copy of the proto tree — rather than the canonical proto/flint/v1/, so it can silently diverge from proto-v1.
failure_scenario: If proto/flint/v1 ever gets a v2 or a fix and the vendored csharp/proto copy is not manually re-synced, the C# SDK generates wire types that no longer match the gateway, causing serialization mismatches that only surface at runtime against production traffic.
evidence: sdks/csharp/FlintSdk/FlintSdk.csproj line 14 `<Protobuf Include="proto/flint/v1/*.proto" .../>`; those .proto files are physically duplicated under sdks/csharp/FlintSdk/proto/flint/v1/ instead of referencing the root proto/ tree.
verify_reason: The finding is real and correctly located. FlintSdk.csproj line 16 (`<Protobuf Include="proto/flint/v1/*.proto" GrpcServices="Client" />`) compiles from a vendored, git-tracked copy of the proto tree at sdks/csharp/FlintSdk/proto/flint/v1/ (6 files) rather than the canonical root proto/flint/v1/. There is NO sync mechanism: dagger/codegen.ts never references or copies proto into the C# SDK, and .github/workflows/ contains zero dotnet/csharp/FlintSdk build steps, so the copy is neither regenerated nor CI-verified. Critically, the drift is no longer hypothetical — it has already occurred: canonical proto/flint/v1/agent.proto was changed on 2026-06-30 (commit a6e0e51) to make RunAgent a bidirectional-streaming RPC (`rpc RunAgent(stream AgentRunRequest) returns (stream AgentEvent)`) with a new `oneof payload { AgentRunStart start; AgentRunControl control }` envelope, while the vendored C# copy is frozen at the 2026-06-19 state (commit 22d8164) with `rpc RunAgent(AgentRunRequest) returns (stream AgentEvent)` (unary request) and is missing the AgentRunStart and AgentRunControl messages entirely. 5 of 6 protos are still byte-identical; agent.proto already diverges on the RPC cardinality and message schema. A C# client generated from the stale copy would open RunAgent as unary-request/server-stream and send a single AgentRunRequest, but the canonical gateway expects a client-streaming channel whose first frame is an AgentRunStart oneof variant — the method descriptors and message schemas mismatch, so every agent-run call from the C# SDK fails at the transport/deserialization layer against production. Severity MEDIUM is appropriate and if anything the characterization is conservative: the auditor said the SDK 'can silently diverge,' but it has already diverged in the committed tree. Kept at MEDIUM (not raised) only because the C# SDK is a near-orphan (not built in CI, one of the less-complete SDKs), bounding blast radius to whoever actually consumes it; for any such consumer it is already broken today.

title: frf-cli crate is completely missing — no operator tooling exists at all

title: /healthz is a static stub that never probes dependencies — a fully-broken gateway reports healthy
defect: healthz() returns a hardcoded `{"status":"ok"}` JSON with zero checks against Iggy, Keto, the JWKS endpoint, or Postgres CDC; there is no /readyz or readiness probe anywhere in the codebase (grep for readyz/readiness across crates/ returns nothing).
failure_scenario: In Kubernetes/load-balancer deployments, the liveness/readiness probe hits /healthz and always gets 200 OK. If the Iggy broker connection dies, Keto becomes unreachable, or the JWKS endpoint is down, the pod stays in rotation and keeps receiving traffic — every publish/subscribe fails at runtime while the orchestrator believes the instance is healthy. No automated failover or restart is triggered; the outage is silent until user-facing errors mount.
evidence: health.rs body is `Json(json!({ "status": "ok", "version": env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION") }))` with no async dependency probe; build_router (lib.rs:64) wires only /healthz, no /readyz.
verify_reason: Verified against actual code. crates/frf-gateway/src/routes/health.rs:4-6 is exactly a hardcoded synchronous-style handler returning Json(json!({ "status": "ok", "version": env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION") })) — it takes no State extractor and performs zero probing of Iggy, Keto, JWKS, or Postgres CDC. build_router (lib.rs:63-64) wires only /healthz among health routes. A grep for readyz|readiness|liveness|/ready across crates/ returns nothing (exit 0, empty), confirming no readiness probe exists anywhere. No port trait (frf-ports/broker-iggy/authz-keto) exposes a health_check/ping method, so nothing is checkable even in principle today. The failure scenario is real and load-bearing, not hypothetical: compose.yml:37-38, compose.override.yml:21-22, and compose.ci.yml:43-44 all wire the container healthcheck to `curl -f http://localhost:8080/healthz`, and dependent services gate startup on it via `depends_on ... condition: service_healthy`. So a gateway with dead Iggy/Keto/JWKS still reports 200/healthy, stays in rotation, and every publish/subscribe fails at runtime with no automated restart or failover. One minor overstatement: a static liveness /healthz is a defensible pattern by itself (liveness intentionally should not fail on downstream outages, to avoid restart storms); the precise defect is the total absence of a readiness (/readyz) probe that gates traffic, not that /healthz itself must probe dependencies. That nuance does not change the outcome. HIGH is correct — a genuine availability/operability hole causing silent degradation and delayed failover, but not CRITICAL (no data loss or security breach).

title: axum HTTP server has no graceful shutdown — in-flight requests and WS streams are dropped on SIGTERM
defect: The HTTP server is started with `axum::serve(listener, app)` inside a tokio::select! that races against ctrl_c; there is no `.with_graceful_shutdown(...)` call, so when ctrl-c fires the select! branch simply drops the serve future. CDC and gRPC tasks get a shutdown signal / abort, but the Axum server and its open WebSocket subscribe streams are terminated abruptly.
failure_scenario: On a rolling deploy or scale-down (SIGTERM/ctrl-c), all active WebSocket subscribers and any in-flight publish requests are cut mid-flight with no drain window. Clients see abrupt disconnects rather than clean close frames, and a publish that was mid-fan-out may be partially delivered. Under Kubernetes rolling updates this happens on every pod cycle.
evidence: main.rs:157-160 `tokio::select! { result = axum::serve(listener, app) => ..., _ = ctrl_c() => ... }` — no with_graceful_shutdown; grep for with_graceful_shutdown across gateway src returns nothing.
verify_reason:
Verified against crates/frf-gateway/src/main.rs:157-160. The finding is accurate. `axum::serve(listener, app)` is invoked inside a `tokio::select!` that races the serve future against `tokio::signal::ctrl_c()`. There is NO `.with_graceful_shutdown(...)` call — grep across the entire gateway src confirms zero occurrences of `with_graceful_shutdown`. When ctrl_c fires, the select! completes the ctrl_c branch and drops the axum serve future immediately, terminating the HTTP server and all open connections abruptly. Long-lived WebSocket streams are genuinely at risk: crates/frf-gateway/src/routes/subscribe.rs (ws_subscribe) and routes/agents.rs are real streaming WS handlers that forward each permitted EventEnvelope as a JSON frame for the lifetime of the subscription. By contrast, the CDC task and gRPC task DO get shutdown coordination (shutdown_tx.send(true) drives cdc via a watch::Receiver at line 162-166; grpc_task.abort() at 167-169) — so the Axum WS path is uniquely un-drained, exactly as described.

Failure scenario is real: on a Kubernetes rolling deploy / scale-down, every SIGTERM/ctrl_c cuts all active WebSocket subscribers mid-stream with no drain window and no clean WS close frames, forcing every client to detect the drop and reconnect on each pod cycle. This is a legitimate production-readiness gap for a real-time fabric.

Severity MEDIUM is correctly calibrated (not higher): the durable event path is the broker (Iggy), and dropping WS delivery does not corrupt persisted state or bypass any authz check — subscribers simply reconnect and resume from offset. The finding's sub-claim that 'a publish mid-fan-out may be partially delivered' is slightly speculative (that IS the abrupt-disconnect symptom, not a separate data-integrity defect), but it does not change the severity. Impact is degraded client experience and reconnect churn, not data loss or a security hole — MEDIUM is right.

title: Config validation checks only env-var presence, not semantic validity — hosted SFU boots with empty LiveKit credentials
defect: GatewayConfig::from_env (config.rs:111) validates presence of a few required env vars but performs no cross-field semantic validation; build_media_signaler in main.rs catches LiveKitSignaling::from_env() failures and falls back to a LiveKitConfig with empty api_key/api_secret/server_url strings, logging only a warn, so a gateway configured SFU_MODE=hosted starts successfully with non-functional media signaling.

evidence: main.rs:315-323 `LiveKitSignaling::from_env().unwrap_or_else(|e| { warn; LiveKitSignaling::new(LiveKitConfig{ api_key: String::new(), api_secret: String::new(), server_url: String::new(), ... }) })`.

title: No broker/checkpoint inspection or debug utility — CDC and sync state cannot be operated at runtime
defect: Checkpoint/offset logic exists inside library crates (frf-app/sync.rs, frf-store-surreal, frf-postgres-cdc/config.rs) but is only reachable from inside the running gateway; there is no CLI or admin endpoint to inspect a replication-slot lag, list broker offsets, reset a stuck CDC slot, or force/inspect a sync checkpoint.
failure_scenario: When the Postgres CDC consumer falls behind or its logical replication slot stalls (a common production failure that pins WAL and can fill the Postgres disk), an operator has no supported tool to inspect slot lag or reset the consumer without restarting the whole gateway. Broker/checkpoint debugging requires attaching to the process or querying Postgres/Iggy directly, with no guardrails.
evidence: grep 'checkpoint' hits only library src files; no binary exposes them; only shell smoke scripts (scripts/smoke-cdc.sh, scripts/bench-regression-check.sh) exist as ops-adjacent tooling.
verify_reason: Every factual claim in the finding is verified against the actual code. (1) No frf-cli crate exists — `ls crates/` shows no frf-cli/frf-sdk-rust; the only binaries in the workspace are frf-gateway and uniffi-bindgen (a codegen helper, not an ops tool). (2) Checkpoint/offset/sync-state logic lives only inside library crates: `grep checkpoint` hits frf-app/src/sync.rs, frf-ports/src/crdt_store.rs, frf-crdt/src/store.rs, frf-store-surreal/src/store.rs, and lsn_checkpoint_interval in frf-postgres-cdc/src/config.rs — none reachable except from inside the running gateway. (3) PostgresCdcConsumer (crates/frf-postgres-cdc/src/consumer.rs) exposes only `new()` and `run_until_shutdown()` — no method to read slot lag, confirmed_flush_lsn, or force a reset. (4) The gateway router (crates/frf-gateway/src/lib.rs:63-91) exposes only /healthz, /v1/subscribe, /v1/publish, /v1/agents, plus dev-only inject endpoints gated behind the dev-endpoints feature — there is NO admin/metrics/slot/lag/checkpoint inspection endpoint, and the gateway Cargo.toml has no metrics/prometheus dependency at all. (5) The only ops-adjacent tooling is two shell scripts (scripts/smoke-cdc.sh, scripts/bench-regression-check.sh); smoke-cdc.sh merely polls pg_replication_slots.active directly via `docker compose exec psql` — a CI smoke check, not an operator inspection/reset tool with guardrails. The production failure scenario is real and well-known: a stalled logical replication slot pins WAL and can fill the Postgres disk; the sync_grpc_service exposes get_checkpoint over gRPC to authenticated clients but there is no operator-facing way to inspect replication-slot lag or reset a stuck CDC consumer without restarting the entire gateway process. The finding is real and correctly characterized as a runtime-operability/observability gap (missing tooling, not a code defect). Severity: the auditor's LOW is defensible for a "missing ops tooling" classification, but given the blast radius (WAL pin → Postgres disk-fill → total outage) with no supported mitigation short of a full gateway restart, MEDIUM is the more accurate severity for a production-release audit.

The gateway genuinely enforces JWT verification on both paths — routes/agents.rs:45 (state.identity.verify(&token).await → 401) and agent_grpc_service.rs:68 — so in a secured (GATEWAY_JWKS_URL) deployment the Agent Activity panel can never connect. Failure scenario is accurate. Two corrections, both of which make the defect worse, not better, so HIGH holds: (1) The WS {type:"auth"} message does NOT authenticate — handle_agent_socket (routes/agents.rs:55-78) never reads inbound socket frames; auth is taken from the HTTP Authorization: Bearer header at upgrade (line 41), which the browser WebSocket constructor (new WebSocket(url, undefined), agentWebSocket.ts:31) cannot set — so the WS agent stream is architecturally unauthenticatable from this UI even if a token existed. Severity HIGH (not CRITICAL): this is a fail-closed defect — the gateway rejects the empty token, so it blocks a feature and reflects an incomplete production auth surface, but admits nothing insecure and leaks no data.

title: Default gateway URL (localhost:4000) mismatches gateway default bind (0.0.0.0:8080)

Every request (Connect subscribe, agent WS, signal WS) targets port 4000 where nothing is bound, producing immediate connection-refused for all four surfaces. The mismatch guarantees a broken out-of-box experience unless the operator happens to set VITE_GATEWAY_URL to :8080.
evidence: gateway.ts:5 `?? "http://localhost:4000"`; features/agents/services/agentWebSocket.ts:5 same default; crates/frf-gateway/src/config.rs:112-113 BIND_ADDR default '0.0.0.0:8080'.
verify_reason: Verified directly against the code. admin-ui/src/infrastructure/gateway.ts:4 defaults GATEWAY_URL to "http://localhost:4000", and the same "http://localhost:4000" default is repeated in agentGrpcStream.ts:16, agentWebSocket.ts:4, and signalingService.ts:4 — all four UI surfaces (Connect subscribe, agent gRPC-web stream, agent WS, signaling WS). Severity HIGH (not CRITICAL) is correct: this is a broken-default / DX defect, not a security or data-loss issue, and it is fixable via one env var.

title: E2E suite only asserts static rendering; all real-connection assertions are skipped in CI
defect: Every integration test is gated by `skipIntegration = SKIP_INTEGRATION === 'true' || !GATEWAY_URL` and test.skip; the signaling spec never asserts a live connection at all (only that inputs/buttons render). No test ever verifies the UI actually receives an event from the gateway, so the connect-failures above pass CI silently.
failure_scenario: CI runs Playwright with no GATEWAY_URL, so all Layer 2 tests skip and only static-render tests run. The team sees green E2E and believes the admin UI is wired to the gateway, while in reality none of the four surfaces can connect. The disconnect ships to production undetected.

The only path that sets GATEWAY_URL=http://localhost:28080 and SKIP_INTEGRATION=false is Stage 10, which is opt-in (ENABLE_INTEGRATION_STAGE=true) and requires DinD with a hardcoded host Docker socket path (line 342), so it does not run in normal hosted CI. playwright.config.ts:16-21 webServer runs `pnpm dev` with no gateway, exactly as claimed. Thus green E2E in mainline CI verifies only static rendering; no test ever confirms the admin UI actually connects to or receives an event from the gateway.
